teaser: Two women, a hot afternoon, nothing happening. Paris was furious.
review_notes:
Catalog year 1857 is the Salon year; the canvas is usually dated 1856-57.
Dimensions about 174 x 206 cm.
Reading of the foreground woman's clothes as underwear (chemise, corset, petticoat) with a shawl thrown over her is the standard account; the exact garments are debated.
The object in the boat is commonly described as a hat, often read as a man's; in this image it is a small pale shape, so the lesson stays cautious.
Gift of the painting to the City of Paris by Juliette Courbet in 1906: please verify.
Courbet's role in the Vendôme Column affair, exile in 1873 and death in 1877: standard biography.

lesson.text: Her eyelids are closing. Not closed: there is still a dark slit between the lashes, and it is aimed at you. The afternoon is hot, the shade under the trees is thick, and she is one breath away from sleep. Gustave Courbet stops the clock right there.

lesson.title: Almost asleep
lesson.text: Three small signs of the same heavy moment.

spots.title: The half-open eye
spots.text: Her cheek is flushed and pressed into the cloth, her lips slightly parted. She notices you watching and cannot be bothered to move.

spots.title: The loose hand
spots.text: The fingers lie open on the patterned fabric, holding nothing. Two gold bracelets circle the wrist. A hand goes slack like this just before sleep.

spots.title: The friend
spots.text: Behind her, a blonde woman props her chin on her hand under a wide hat. She is awake, and she stares off to the left at something we will never see.

lesson.text: That is the whole event. Nobody speaks, nobody looks at anybody, no story unfolds. And Courbet painted it big: about 174 x 206 cm (5.7 x 6.8 ft), so the women are close to life size. In 1857 a canvas that large was meant for kings, battles or saints.

Then there was the title. “Demoiselles” sounds polite, like “young ladies”, but visitors to the Paris Salon, the huge official exhibition of the year, heard the irony. Everything suggested these two were not respectable girls of good family. The first clue was what the dark-haired one has on.

lesson.title: Dressed, or undressed?
lesson.text: Read her outfit from the shoulder down to the feet.

spots.title: Thin white cotton
spots.text: A light bodice with a lace-edged sleeve and a pale ribbon. To eyes of 1857 this was underwear. She has taken off her dress and lies on the grass in what goes beneath it.

spots.title: The shawl
spots.text: A long shawl with a red flowered border has been thrown across her. Shawls like this were costly, the kind of gift a woman might get from a wealthy lover.

spots.title: Petticoats
spots.text: Layers of white frills spill over the grass. Courbet paints each scallop of lace with thick, creamy strokes, as solid as whipped cream.

spots.title: Boots and stockings
spots.text: Two brown ankle boots and white stockings stick out of the froth, one above the other. Showing a woman's ankles was already improper.

lesson.text: The Salon was full of naked women, but they were called Venus or nymphs and lived in a dreamland. A modern Parisian in her underthings, with a hint of sweat on her face, was something else. Critics called the picture vulgar and the women ugly, heavy, even dirty.

Courbet was used to trouble. Two years earlier, when the jury of the 1855 World's Fair refused some of his canvases, he rented a plot nearby, built his own pavilion, and charged admission to a one-man show under a single word: Realism.

Realism, for him, meant painting only what he could see in his own time: workers, villagers, a funeral in his home town. No angels, he said, because he had never seen one. Here he applies that rule to pleasure and to boredom.
How did the women get to this bank, so far from the boulevards? Courbet leaves an answer in the background, half hidden by the leaves, and with it a small mystery that has never been settled.
The two friends did not walk here. Find how they arrived.

spots.title: The rowboat
spots.text: A brown boat is pulled up against the bank, oars shipped. Something pale lies inside it, usually described as a hat.

lesson.text: Many viewers have read that hat as a man's. If so, a third person rowed them here and has stepped away for a moment. Or he stands exactly where you stand, and the sleepy look is for him. Courbet never said. The picture works like a trap either way.

The anarchist thinker Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, a friend of Courbet, defended the painting as a moral lesson about idle luxury. Courbet himself seems to have enjoyed painting the lace far too much for that.

There was also something new in the subject. Railways had just made the riverbanks outside Paris a cheap Sunday escape for city people. Courbet was among the first to treat that leisure as worthy of a major canvas. A few years later Manet set his own scandalous picnic by the water, and then came the Impressionists.

spots.title: Wildflowers
spots.text: The blonde woman's arm rests on a heap of flowers picked along the bank: yellow, white, blue. They sit in the lap of her dark red dress.

spots.title: A lace mitten
spots.text: Her hand hangs out of a black lace mitten that leaves the fingers bare, a fashionable accessory of the 1850s.

spots.title: The hanging bonnet
spots.text: A bonnet trimmed with flowers and ribbons has been hooked on the branches at the right. It probably belongs to the sleeper, set aside with her dress.

spots.title: The Seine
spots.text: The river is painted in flat, pale blues with a strip of far bank. It is the only cool, open part of the canvas.

spots.title: The leaf ceiling
spots.text: Dark oak leaves close over the women like a lid and press the scene toward you. Courbet often laid in foliage like this with a palette knife, a small flat blade.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: In the bottom left corner, in red on the green grass: G. Courbet.

lesson.text: Courbet's taste for provocation ended badly. Blamed for the toppling of the Vendôme Column in Paris during the uprising of 1871, he was jailed, then billed for rebuilding it. He fled to Switzerland in 1873 and died there four years later.
His sister Juliette kept guard over his reputation for decades. In 1906 she gave this canvas to the City of Paris, which is why it hangs in the Petit Palais today.

Go back to the eye that is almost shut. Nothing has changed, and yet you now know she is in her underwear, in a size meant for heroes, with a boat waiting and a hat that may not be hers. The laziest afternoon in French painting was a carefully planned attack.

quiz.question: Why did the size of the canvas bother people in 1857?
options: Such a large format was meant for noble subjects
It was too small to see at the Salon
It was painted on several panels
quiz.explanation: A canvas over two meters wide was expected to show history, religion or kings.

quiz.question: What is the dark-haired woman wearing?
options: Her undergarments, with a shawl thrown over them
quiz.explanation: She has taken off her dress and lies in thin white cotton and petticoats.

quiz.question: What is found in the background, pulled up to the bank?
options: A rowboat with a hat in it
quiz.explanation: The boat tells how they came and hints at a possible third person.

quiz.question: What did Courbet do when the 1855 World's Fair jury refused some of his works?
options: He stopped painting for a year
He built his own pavilion and held a solo show
He repainted them as mythological scenes
quiz.explanation: He opened a one-man exhibition under the word Realism.

quiz.question: What did Realism mean for Courbet?
options: Painting only what he could see in his own time
Painting scenes from ancient history accurately
quiz.explanation: He painted contemporary life and refused subjects he had never seen.

facts.text: The woman in the foreground is fast asleep with her eyes shut.
facts.explanation: Her eyes are half open and turned toward the viewer.

facts.text: Courbet's sister gave the painting to the City of Paris.
Critics at the Salon praised the two women as models of elegance.
facts.explanation: They called the picture vulgar and the women ugly and heavy.
